Initially, a thorough analysis of existing HR systems and recruitment tool functionalities is essential. This includes evaluating data structures, communication protocols, and security measures. Data mapping is crucial, ensuring that information from recruitment tools, such as candidate profiles and application status, aligns accurately with corresponding HR system fields. Continuous testing is imperative to identify and rectify potential issues, ensuring a smooth data flow. User training is essential to familiarize HR teams with the integrated system. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-01-04", "text": "Well, it's not super clear what you want... Do you want a filter and chiller - or just filtered drinking water? And assuming you are just replacing your Brita, I take it that a carbon filter is fine - you aren't looking for reverse osmosis water. For carbon filtered drinking water I would suggest two choices: 1. install a filter housing and then acarbon filter to go in it. (less expensive and very flexible).  About $100 for housing, filter and mounting bracket. title: Architect designs failed zoning review - how should we respond? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-852293901", "author_name": "E C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-852293901", "date": "2024-01-04", "text": "We live on a corner lot and have spent the last two years working on an addition design that faces the street side of our home (not the front entry, the garage side). We moved out in early December, with plans for demo to take place in mid-December. Design plans for code review had been submitted in early November. Just prior to the Christmas holiday we learned our plans did not comply with zoning ordinances. The issue is that the city defines unpermissable demolition as \"razing, tearing down, or demolishing a street facing wall.\" This is the wall that would need to be taken down to accommodate the new addition. After a great deal of obfuscation and confusion, we learned that the zoning denial was related to this definition, of which our design team was unaware. The team contends that this is an \"interpretation\" by the city - but the language is just as I wrote above, not ambiguous - the demolition of a street-facing wall is considered a full tear down. Further complicating the situation - if our team *had* understood the code, and gone through a conditional use permit request to allow for the demolition - the resulting build would fall under \"new construction\" which kicks off an entirely new set of zoning requirements to which our designs do not comply. Our question is: How severe of an oversight was the misunderstanding of \"demolition\" by our design team? They claim that they \"learn the code by experience and this is the first time they have encountered this issue\". Bear in mind that this is a leading firm with price points to match that reputation. In my research to understand what happened (the designer's explanation was insufficient for us to comprehend what had taken place), the language of the code is not only unambiguous - it is the lead paragraph on the section dedicated to demolition. The designer's contention is that the city didn't flag the zoning error in earlier conversations (which, I believe were related to confirming setbacks) and that the city's \"interpretation\" of the code is the source of the problem. I'd appreciate your feedback on whether this is just \"one of those things\" or if it exceeds the acceptable bounds of professional practice.", "images": []}

title: Underlayment or second layer of subfloor? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rezaulk", "author_name": "Rezaul Khan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rezaulk", "date": "2024-01-05", "text": "So, I have been doing a lot of research and could not find a solid answer. There seems to be different opinions. For my half-bathroom renovation, I am starting fresh. For flooring, for the first layer I am using 23/32 Advantech T&G, which is glued to the joists and then screwed down with 1-3/4\" screws. Now, I want to install a second layer, 3/4\" plywood, to meet the minimum 1-1/8\" thickness for the large format porceline tiles I picked out. Now, what I came across is that some people claim this second layer to be \"underlayment\" and some argues that it is still subfloor (second layer of subfloor) -- and with that, they offer two different installation methods: Method 1: If it's underlayment, then you don't glue the second layer to the first layer, and should use a shorter screw (1-1/4\") to fasten the 3/4\" ply to the first layer without fastening to the joists. And maybe put some kind of felt paper in between the boards (optional). Method 2: if it's the second layer of the subfloor, then you glue in between the boards, and use longer screws so the second layer, 3/4\" ply, can also be fastened to the joists. I understand the installation method, but I can't figure out what I am doing would be considered underlayment or second layer of subfloor? I will also laydown 1/4\" uncoupling membrane (Schluter Ditra) on top of the ply before installing the tile.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "klem1", "author_name": "klem1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/klem1", "date": "2024-01-05", "text": "First things first.   Are you SURE what you see in lines is tree roots?   Bio-mass gardually grows inside septic lines to the point it renders field lines usless so that line replacement in a new location is required.  The stuff resembles tiny roots on a scope but easily distingused when pulled from line on snake.   how long has it been since tanks were pumped?   Are you sure pumper is finding ALL tanks.  Many systems have up to 3 tanks.  for now I'll assume this isn't bio-mass but if you decide that's what it is just say so and we can work on solutions. If roots are between house and cleanout you can get more bang from root killer.   At a time when little or no water will be dumped into lines,  block line at cleanout with something similar to this.   After line is blocked put your root killer in drain and use enough water to flush it down to and fill pipe above block.  You might pour 5 gallons or until water backs up in tub drain.   You can see that if killer just making contact with roots as it flows past roots as directed on product kills roots having killer stand in contact with roots for 2 or 3 hours should result in far more roots being killed.   I wouldn't think it neccessary for killer to stand more than overnight.   An alternate or additional remedy is putting killer in a root feeder similar to this and inject into soil near line in attempt to kill roots BEFORE they enter line.  Killer lingers in soil whereas when used as directed on container killer briefly contacts roots then flushed out into field which isn't bad if you happen to have roots out there as  well. houzz wouldn't allow link to root feeder so just look for Ross Root Feeder at big box or garden center.", "images": []}}

I am trying to be thorough. Plenty of people, both men and women, find themselves in a similar situation.  Unfortunately, it seems all too common for contractors to underbid jobs or oversell their quality in an effort to get your signature on the contract. So first, I am concerned about the job growing from $20,000 to $42,000.  There may be legitimate reasons for that, but often it is more than a little sketch.  Moreover, while most clients just pay to get out of the ordeal there are often legal protections in place if the consumer is willing to take advantage of them.  So what state are you in? There are basically three types of contracts (1) fixed-price, (2) cost-plus, and (3) time and materials. In a fixed-price contract the $20,000 would have been the price to complete all work they were contracted to complete.  Fixed-price contracts can grow as the scope of the work changes but typically these changes have to be handled via change orders, which are basically smaller fixed-price contracts that should be presented prior to the work beginning but when necessary may be presented shortly after that work is commences.  So in a fixed price contract you should be able to calculate the entire price of the job as the original contract plus all change orders provided in a timely manner.  In a fixed price contract you generally have the right to see all the change orders but no other detailed billing. In a cost plus contract the contractor's duty to the client is a bit higher because the client is absorbing more price risk.  In these contracts the work is done at cost and the contractor adds a fee (often a %) for the management of that work. In contract law \"cost\" has a very specific meaning... it is the amount actually paid less any discounts or rebates.  So in a cost-plus contract if the contractor pays a subcontractor $1,200 but gets $100 rebate then he must bill you $1,100 plus his fee calculated on that $1,100.  Because there is a higher level of trust in a cost-plus contract, the customer has the right to see all invoices that were paid to suppliers and subcontractors, and even the right to verify those amounts. A time and materials contract is most suited when one firm will do all the work without subcontractors.  Typically, these contracts are materials at cost and labor at a specified unit rate.  These types of contracts are often abused for several reasons.  Contractors often just add mark-up to their materials rather than passing along the actual legal contract.  Contrary to popular belief time and materials contracts are not actually for the time spent on the job, they are actually for the time reasonable and necessary to complete the job.  So a contractor can't take 14 hours to complete a 4 hour job and just bill you the extra amount.  Because they are the most abused they are also the most regulated by states and some states (California for example) have banned time and materials contracts for home improvements.  In a time and materials contract you have the right to a complete breakdown of that job, the time that job took, and the materials used. ---- Now for the next part... Getting help with assessing the work.  I have never found it particularly difficult to get one contractor to talk bad about another contractor's work.  I have found it difficult to get something in writing.  So I advise looking for someone to repair the work rather than someone to help you prepare for a meeting.  Simply note that you want to know what is wrong and what it is going to cost to make it right.  Leave your new contractor out of the dispute with the other contractor.  I have had really good luck with recommendations from lumber yards (not big box stores... actual lumber yards).  They interact with most contractors and will often tell you who they hold in high regard and may be able to tell you who they think may be willing to do it. Take notes on what this contractor tells you is wrong and use those notes in your discussion with your existing contractor.  If your existing contractor disagrees with the assessment simply ask them to put it in writing.  Making a contractor memorialize things is often pretty effective at cutting through the B.S.  It is easy to tell you a lie when there is no proof of it, however, that lie in an email can be used against them and they know it.  You can do this in a confrontational way and simply say I don't trust anything you are unwilling to write in an email or text, or the non-confrontational way and pretend you just want it in writing so you can understand it better because you are a bit confused. main_question: {"author_id": "kookygravy", "author_name": "Kooky Gravy", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kookygravy", "date": "2024-01-05", "text": "Hi everyone, First-time poster and long-time lurker of the discussion boards here! I'm trying to gather as much information as possible, and hopefully help others wondering the same things. We have a full interior remodel in progress and our engineered hardwood is currently being installed. I would be grateful for feedback on whether or not I should worry about some aspects of the job so far. Gallery with images of concerns: https://postimg.cc/gallery/V89DJ13X Relevant Details Concerns Again, any comments and feedback are appreciated! Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1829880277", "author_name": "G & S Floor Service", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1829880277", "date": "2024-01-08", "text": "Having less joints makes  for a better  rigid floor assembly.  Joints are weak spots. This is usually where problems occur first.   Having single length boards, you have deferred these problem areas to the perimeters of the room. Which reduces your problem areas. You're not dealing with bad mill work, bad cuts or carfstmanship.  Example: your first two photos. Single length floor boards will help keep your surface flatter. Less joints, less over and under wood, a more flatter and even floor.  Example: your mitered transition. A lot of old homes use single length floor boards.  These floors have stood the test of time. The reason why it is not used too often these days is cost.  It takes too much time and raw material to come up with select or clear grade flooring. Which drives up the cost. Also, delivery is a pain trying to mauever 16 ft. length bundles around the house/job-site. Regarding your closet, it's a small walk-in. Most of your floors will get covered with built-ins and items along the walls. you will probably end up with a 2x3 area left of visible flooring. It will look worst with a bunch of joints. What you have is fine.  You can tell the contractor, that you want visible staggered joints for the remaining of the project. Otherwise, whenever and wherever you can use single length boards, do so. You will have a flatter and stronger floor.  Especially for glue-downs and floating installations.", "images": []}}

title: Experiments and Orders | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "migreenthumb", "author_name": "MiGreenThumb (Z5b S.Michigan/Sunset 41) Elevation: 1091 feet", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/migreenthumb", "date": "2024-01-05", "text": "Good afternoon everyone! I thought I would share a little bit of plant cheer especially for us Northerners as we approach the depths of winter. Always forging ahead, bucking conventional \"wisdom\", I also have some plant thrills to share.My Impatients are an autumn rescue from my old garden in 2021 and need repotting again, the Phalaenopsis is opening blooms on a new stalk after the old fades, and a third old stalk is attempting to branch again as well. It's going on 8 years old, and will soon be in bloom most of the year. The aloe is going bananas and needs potted up. My pineapple top I rooted is still trucking along and getting ever more serrated. The poinsettia is one I kept from a year ago Christmas. Shame on me, but it's still in its same container and mix. I never fertilized it. Never regulated it's daylight or darkness hours. And yet... It still coloured up before December 15th.I'm working on my second, and most likely final order of 2024, and it will be from Roses Unlimited. I've agonized over my final selections to stay in budget, but a few are for sure: Alchymist, Mirandy, Sutter's Gold, Souvenir d'Alphonse Lavallee, and Starfire. Florence Delattre is most likely another finalized selection. I was disappointed that Charlotte Armstrong, \u00c9toile de Hollande (bush form, as noted by the lack of \"Cl\"), King's Ransom, and a few others aren't listed this year! Mid-Century Moderns are my weakness.Now, for the thrills! Bucking all things I have heard regarding having roses indoors as they are outdoor animals, I am keeping two potted roses in my heated basement that used to be a finished living room over the winter. Since I put up a better grow light that a buddy of mine used to grow cannabis (Michigan, don'tcha know!), they haven't just survived since October, but don't seem to be hating it and struggling, either. They are located near two windows, the electric baseboard heater, across the room from the LP forced air heat, and with a dehumidifier set to 40%. They are Mrs. Sam McGredy and Lady Emma Hamilton. LEH has a bud that has been developing since shortly before Christmas and is about fully open, smelling as divinely as she should. Mrs. Sam though not setting buds, as I expect it not to, has pushed all kinds of new growth with beautiful, healthy leaves. No bugs, no mildew, no crisping and shrivelling. I do partly suspect she may be the climbing version because she was from Rogue Valley Roses and even in full sunlight outdoor she started throwing awfully long canes but does bloom on new wood. If anyone happens to have experience with this lovely Pernetiana, I would love to hear about it.Have I somehow discovered a magic spec combination that the roses do not hate? I am planning on adding another grow light but have been pleasantly surprised at the decent progress and not to mere survival I've observed since I have brought them indoors in October!Happy gardening and cheers to being different,Steven", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ef41639305987a94_1696-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ff21f93305987acf_1729-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1b21e91a05987b13_1798-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1411963405987b41_1847-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/33514fb505987b89_1916-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

main_question: {"author_id": "jrb451", "author_name": "jrb451", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jrb451", "date": "2024-01-06", "text": "A few years back we tore out the rotting timbers on the elevated beds off our terrace, replaced with stacking block, and added new garden soil, which was a composted mixture from a nursery. The plants - daylilies, annuals, roses, Irises, etc. grow well but I was wondering if adding in earthworms would further benefit the growing environment. Has anyone done this, with good results? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mad-gallica", "author_name": "mad_gallica (z5 Eastern NY)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mad-gallica", "date": "2024-01-10", "text": "I do not have native worms. They were killed off by the glaciers of the last ice age, and have yet to repopulate this far north. They are on their way, but worms move slowly. Currently, most of our worms are European, and reasonably benign. However, right now the NYS DEC is having hissy fits over Asian Jumping Worms, which are an invasive species  capable of causing major environmental issues. Because of the historic lack of native worms, the forests of the northern northeast have adapted to a very slow decomposition of organic matter, and these invasive worms quickly chew up the leaf debris. So, as usual, the answer is It Depends, and what is mostly depends on is where in the world you are. title: Do you have friends who are not supportive of your build? | Houzz Forum

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "k-brown73", "author_name": "Keen B", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/k-brown73", "date": "2024-01-08", "text": "What Chispa said...people get bored, or simply cannot fathom why every single detail is so important to you.  But there are a few who are jealous as others have said here; they do not understand the financials of it all and make huge assumptions on what it would take for THEM to do what you are doing.  I lean on my Houzz community for that reason...I cannot talk openly about some of the burdens and joys of building. My DH and I now own three homes.  From the outside, it looks like we are rolling in dough.  One is our primary residence that we chose primarily because it was a very low-priced victim of the 2008 housing crash, and we could pay it off quickly.  It's a 1978  3/4 and a door, nothing fancy, but we fixed it up and love it.  One is a mountain cabin that we bought with 4 other families; we paid  off our portion in ten years.  The other is our retirement home that we are currently finishing, which will not be paid off any time soon unless we sell the other two. And we are paying far less than many because we are doing it ourselves.  All three combined cost less than some of the homes my friends live in...  Am I going to go into all that with the few people who express their envy? I have to squelch that urge all the time. I want to tell the one with the huge brick home in the gated, golf, country club community that maybe she could afford all three if she didn't have a $1000 month HOA on top of her mortgage whenever she makes passive aggressive remarks.  I want to tell the other that it could be done if she didn't get new, big ass, high end SUVs every few years. (I drive my cars into the 200k mile range, til they drop from under me.) whenever she moans that she's not so lucky.  I want to tell my sister-in-law (who lost her beach house in a foreclosure) that she should have listened to us then and made better financial decisions with other components in her life.  BUT I don't... My friends prefer the clubs and the high end cars, and dinners out and fancy clothes,  just like your friend prefers the expensive vacations...they just don't like they have to have limits, rather than having it all. We knew we would have hard water, so we paid a professional water treatment company many thousands to have a softener system with purified drinking water for our kitchen. A few months after moving in, I noticed my blonde hair (professionally bleached) was turning green \ud83d\udc9a \ud83d\ude29. I called the water treatment company and they sent technicians out to test everything. All tests came back normal -- no copper, no chlorine, normal pH, blah blah blah. I tried a special shower head, that helped a little. The house is 3 floors, including basement (where our master suite is) and I tried using a different shower. Still green, but turned more slowly. Through so much googling, I tried shutting off the recirculating pump. If it hasn't bloomed often, give it lots of water in the summer, trim it in the fall and heap leaves over it in the winter, to mulch it.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "luis-pr", "author_name": "luis_pr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/luis-pr", "date": "2024-01-08", "text": "It sounds like this shrub is a type of hydrangea that may already have developed dormant, spring 2024 flower buds at the ends of the stems. Big Leaf and Mountain Hydrangeas, which typically produce mophead form blooms or lacecap form blooms, do that and they should be planted where they can attain their estimated size at maturity (height/width) and then they should be rarely pruned to control size. These types of hydrangeas develop dormant, spring 2024 flower buds anywhere from July through September-ish 2023 inside the stem ends and the buds then open and resemble tiny broccoli heads in 2024. Under normal conditions, the bud at the end of the stem typically opens and blooms but, there are back up flower buds located lower down the stem that can also open if the one at the end gets killed by late frosts/pruning stems prematurely/etc. The leafless stems of these two types of hydrangeas should not be pruned now as they are currently loaded with dormant, flower buds. If they still remain leafless by the end of June (or maybe even wait until July if near Canada), you can then prune them all the way down. Pruning these types of hydrangeas to control their size is typically tricky and risky. Prune at the wrong time and you get no spring blooms. The incredible number of threads - especially of late,  asking \"what about this foyer, what about these windows, how do I remodel this kitchen..... \" The same kitchen where you've not yet unpacked a single fork! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dadoes", "author_name": "dadoes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dadoes", "date": "2024-01-10", "text": "It's for handling stains and soils that respond accordingly to heat.  The onboard heating element heats the water to generate steam, which emanates through the drum perforations.  Temperature choices are unavailable being that the machine must control the temp to a specific target to produce the steam.  The fill level (in the outer tub) is minimal during the steam process so there's less volume of water to be heated. Steam is at the same *temperature* (212\u00b0F) as boiling water, but steam contains more heat *energy* to vaporize the water.  Delicates or items subject to heat damage reasonably shouldn't be exposed to the steam. Steam option esseentially ends up heating the wash water to between 150 and 158 degrees.  Selecting  the steam option also removes any variation of soil level.  Please ask further questions if you want to know more.", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "doreycrouse", "author_name": "doreycrouse", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/doreycrouse", "date": "2024-01-24", "text": "Sienna, Depending on the machine, most will start with a warm wash and heat the water to a higher temperature with a built in heating element. This does increase stain removal by a wide margin, but is not ideal for a majority of loads. The long wash time increases wear, the heat can cause fading for dark items, and energy use is increased. Though, it does increase removal of greasy or oily stains. I like to run the steam option on rags because of this, however when this option is selected you can not run a prewash. Some machines 'generate' steam and inject it into the tub, like DADoES said, which IMHO doesn't do very much. Consumer Reports tested the steam cycles on some unspecified washers about 10 years ago and found that the increase in cleaning performance was minimal compared to the increase in energy consumption and cycle time. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1477504407", "author_name": "Ian Green Garden and Landscape Design", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1477504407", "date": "2024-01-12", "text": "Most of what Chris said is correct, but reducing your mowing height is not. There are hundreds of types of grass seed and seed mixes for lawns, different types of grass have different mowing heights, i.e., look at golf courses, you have the rough, longer grasses, the fairway, medium cut and the greens cut very short. I would always recommend leaving your grass cut height for a garden lawn to a minimum of 20mm. Two reasons for this, one, grass is a plant and it needs to photosynthesise and for this it needs leaves, if you keep chopping of the blades of grass to short, you are reducing its leaves and it will become weak over time, and thus you will have to keep feeding and watering more. Second, leaving the grass that bit longer will stop light reaching the ground and will prevent a lot of weeds germinating as the longer grass will smother them out and it will need less watering. Besides, when ever you cut your lawn, when cut long or shortish it will always look smart. If you really want a short lawn get the right grass seed mix, but beware, the shorter the grass, the more maintenance is required to keep it looking good. Ian", "images": []}}

title: Tree fell on my house yesterday | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "erasmus-gw", "author_name": "erasmus_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/erasmus-gw", "date": "2024-01-10", "text": "We had  a big storm system yesterday like a lot of other people in the SE and Eastern US.   Mainly it was a steady rain but we got some wind.  I was upstairs reading and didn't hear it but my husband said the  rain was blowing sideways at one point.   When the rain stopped I went outside to look around and at first I thought the damage was minor...a few medium sized limbs down,  lots of twigs and small stuff,   plastic tub blown a ways.   Then I went into the back yard and a very tall Leyland Cypress had crashed into our house.  I didn't even hear it.  Neither did my husband.   I mean,  it is leaning against the house but I don't think it has  damaged it much.  The smaller branches  are keeping the trunk off of the house.    I hope they get it off our house before the small branches break. Three other Leyland Cypresses lower in my garden are leaning.   On two of them the soil is raised a couple of feet with the roots  almost  out of the ground.  One is leaning towards the street.   We called the town,  a tree service,  and our insurance and all will be out here today.   I planted all those Leylands many years ago thinking they were shrubs.  They ended up very tall trees.   I am not good at  estimating feet but they look like they're 60 or 70'  tall.   We had  8 removed last year but left a few for a little privacy. The tree guys last year said that by far the most of their business involves cutting down Leyland Cypresses.   They are  shallow rooted and not long lived and they get very tall.   For years I  appreciated mine as they  provided privacy and  nice evergreen  border for my garden.   Removing 8 of them last year let in a lot more light so there was that. title: January:  hello from the fishbowl | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2024-01-10", "text": "Here is one of the neighbor's calves, staring in our living room window as our cats and we stare back.  The neighbors let their calves run free for a while until they stall them for milk production.  They wander over the fields and through our garden, file down through the woods exploring, lollop down the tractor road to the farther fields.  I suspect this is great for the calves' health and happiness, but it used to infuriate me:  the deep hoofprints they dig into wet clay paths, and the damage they do stumbling over low slopes and through shrubs, and their occasional experimental plant sampling.  However, it eventually occurred to me that cows eat mainly grass, and that they were both mowing and fertilizing the garden.  So I became more accepting.  And it is pleasant to see livestock living free for a while and enjoying themselves. January has not been tremendously cheery here.  I caught a cold/virus/something shortly before Christmas which I haven't yet shaken off, while DH and DD are both tired, coldish, and generally feeling vaguely poorly.  The weather has been nasty for quite a while, first gray, then raining, now rawly cold, as we wimpy residents of this part of the world define cold.  The rain, though it kept us somnolent in the house, was fabulous as far as precipitation is concerned.  It rained!  Possibly two inches, though I didn't measure it.  I don't know what it did for groundwater levels, but the garden certainly got watered. I get out when the weather permits and do cleanup in the garden; also, in spite of my oft-repeated resolve never to plant after the start of the new year, DH and I have planted a few things.  I had DH dig up some starts of flowering ash and oak seedlings to plant in an open area that I want to turn into a pocket woodland.  This casual effort may not work:  if it doesn't, try again with more preparation next time.  I've continued my interminable hedging with a few plants, more to get them out of their pots, where I have to protect them from cold, than from eagerness to have them in the ground.  It's pleasant, as always, to see how the roses are doing and greet them as I work on them. There's a little in bloom:  the native Helleborus foetidus is opening its lime-green flowers; and the green snowdrops (Galanthus woronowii) in the woods are up and showing their buds.  I like the green snowdrops, but they're not what I ordered, which was the native snowdrop, G. nivalis.  I wanted native flowers for the woods, but had planted them all over before I discovered they were the wrong species.  They're spreading like mad, too.  Oh, well.  I'm still waiting for the common snowdrops, which I do have some of, to show, and their double forms:  they should bloom in January, too.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b3520849059ebce9_1946-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

However I am the accident prone type so I want to have some confidence that these aren\u2019t easily stained.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6d92cd90059f14ae_4336-w500-h446-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kmcgowan35", "author_name": "chicagoans", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kmcgowan35", "date": "2024-01-10", "text": "I went down quite a rabbit hole reading about PEI (Porcelain Enamel Institute) ratings and water absorption classifications for tile, but many tile sites don't provide those ratings and classifications on their websites anyway. I would recommend ordering plenty of samples and testing them: leave spots of red sauce, olive oil, soy sauce, lemon juice, etc. overnight, and see how they clean up. You may also want to leave a tile half submerged in water to see whether it absorbs. Keep a fresh tile for comparing. Also, if you are looking for a very consistent look like your inspiration picture, be sure to check the variation level of the tile (V1 - V4, V1 is the lowest.) Because of this, it is on the historic registry, but that only legally restricts us from changing the exterior. House was built with cement cast \"stones\" and has a foursquare floorplan with many craftsman style details. The kitchen is in the back of the house, behind the dining room. Updates have already been made over the years, so most of the woodwork has been painted (not by me!), and an addition was done at some point which added several bathrooms. The kitchen is in need of an update, the cabinets I think are 1970ish in age and tile countertops are cracking, and the floors are covered in peel and stick tiles (maybe there is wood underneath? So we plan to redo the kitchen. The adjacent dining room is charming, with wainscoting, corner cabinets, wallpaper, more natural light, original wood floors and possibly an original fireplace hiding behind a wall but we have not gone exploring in the walls yet. I am considering whether it would be ok to open up the wall between the kitchen and dining room. We are a family of 4 with youngish kids and the kitchen as it is now is very isolated, I would like for there to be more ability to have a conversation with someone sitting in the dining room. Would it be a bad idea to tear the wall between them down? Or even to create just a pass through? I appreciate the character of the home of course otherwise I would not have bought it but it IS inconvenient to have the kitchen all closed up and hidden in the back. One person I was chatting with told me it ruined the character of the historic home when people open up separate rooms....But also we live here and I think the renovation would create a beautiful space, that I like to think could be done carefully to respect the historic character. title: Total Renovation & Addition - 1963 Brick Ranch | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "suze425", "author_name": "Susan W", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/suze425", "date": "2024-01-12", "text": "Hello - we\u2019re embarking on a major renovation project and this is going to be my place to chronicle our progress. I have a couple of threads over on the Kitchens forum, as that was one of the major things we tackled in Phase 1 of our complete house renovation, and I started 1 or 2 threads in the very early stages of Phase 2, about 9 months ago. We\u2019ve had the house since June of 2021, started Phase 1 in June of 2022, moved in in November of 2022, and here we are finally breaking ground for Phase 2 in January 2024. It\u2019s been a process. Backstory: We purchased the house, located on the Gulf Coast of Mississippi, from the estate of our next door neighbor after he died. It was truly a hot mess - filthy, stuffed with junk (as in hoarder house), totally overgrown yard, and filled with Chinese drywall from after Hurricane Katrina (2005.) But it\u2019s on a relatively large lot for the area, we love the neighborhood in this little beach town, and it definitely had some decent bones. 'Russelliana' is listed as a hybrid Multiflora, a group that has a bad history in my garden, but then along comes this variety and blows my doubts away.  It's growing in rocky clay, sometimes very wet, and seems entirely happy.  (The wet may be advantageous:  it's a stronger plant than the other two I have growing in heavy, more droughty ground.)  My plant has been in place a dozen years of so.  It has never gotten above shrub size in its starveling conditions, but in the last year or so has begun putting out longer canes, as if it might build in time to become a climber.  One thing I notice about it is that it seems to be very little troubled by cane damage--I mean, it experiences cane damage, but the cane is not overly bothered by it--and also has long-lived canes.  I don't recall seeing foliage disease, either.  All in all, a handsome rose to plant and then not worry about, and know that it will do you proud.  Oh, and it roots easily. My question follows.  Many roses sucker out and make new canes from below the ground, including many of the once-flowering old roses:  Gallicas, Albas, Foetidas, and others. If I'm getting them in east Tennessee, a lot of folks are also going to share the misery. As will their plants. A warning from a seller of fruit trees strongly suggested bending new ones over and covering with four to five inches of soil. Derzeit w\u00fcrde man sich in den bereichen bewegend nur den R\u00fccken zukehren. Da\u00df das keine Einheit bildet ist klar. Eine gelungene Aufteilung k\u00f6nnte die sein, da\u00df man auf der einben Seite eine reine Arbeitsk\u00fcche mit Arbeitsplatz und etwas Ger\u00e4tefl\u00e4che schafft, w\u00e4hrend dem gegen\u00fcber die Lagerk\u00fcche aufgestellt wird, die aufgrund ihrer Gr\u00f6\u00dfe sogar eine ausgelagerte Kaffeebar haben k\u00f6nnte, da\u00df auch diese Ger\u00e4te (und Tassen und Zubeh\u00f6r) nicht die Arbeitsk\u00fcche belasten. *****   Ein L\u00f6sungsansatz mit mehreren Details, die f\u00fcreinander wichtig sind. Ein M\u00f6bel, an das man herantritt, oder aben bewusst drumherumgeht. main_question: {"author_id": "chirag-shah32", "author_name": "Chirag Shah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chirag-shah32", "date": "2024-01-15", "text": "Hi guys, We moved into our new construction house in July. Our humidity is 30% according to a manual hygrometer (38% according to NEST). Temps are 68-70 degrees inside, and -10 outside. Every single elevate window has ice on the bottom and condensation all around. Marvin says its a humidity problem, but I am wondering if it is a Elevate series problem in this weather. I will say, our door from a different company also got ice on it. My drapes are open to allow for air to circulate. My humidifiers are off (I have 2 furnaces in the home).", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/26124c8c05a54680_0306-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/bb924bc205a54681_0308-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/528254d405a54683_0308-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/88d24d3b05a54684_0312-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oberon476", "author_name": "oberon476", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oberon476", "date": "2024-01-15", "text": "With indoor temperature of 70\u00b0 and 38% Rh, the dew point temp would be around 43\u00b0. With outside air at -10\u00b0, then the edge temperature of the window glass should be around 35\u00b0 or so, or 8\u00b0 below the dew point temperature. However, since you have ice on the lower edges of the windows, they are below below freezing at the bottom edge. Because of the design of the window wall the bottom edge of both the lower windows (floor level) and upper windows (resting on the cross beam) are going to be colder than they would be in a different set-up. This combined with very cold outside air plus excess humidity (or so the windows think), results in significant water and ice on the (especially) lower edges of the windows. Given the conditions that you describe, you would need windows with a Condensation Resistance Factor of around 70 to avoid or seriously limit window condensation. This is possible with triple pane windows, but not any dual pane that I am aware of. If you have dual panes without a surface 4 coating, your windows are probably have a CRF of 50 or so, but if you have dual pane glass with a surface 4 coating then potentially looking at low 40's CRF. If you could lower your indoor Rh to around 20%, by removing moisture, not warming the air, then you would be approaching the Rh level you would need to be at to avoid condensation, but that's not very realistic. IMO a better approach might be to try to warm the windows by using a couple of fans to blow room air over the glass or even using small space heaters to warm the glass, at least until the below zero temps have moved on. . +1 to Wow's reply, I didn't see it until after I posted, but agree 100%.", "images": []}}

title: Mixed results with meal delivery service | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "originalpinkmountain", "author_name": "l pinkmountain", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/originalpinkmountain", "date": "2024-01-15", "text": "So early on this year, I was reflecting on how I might improve my life situation in 2024.  As a thought exercise, I used a technique I learned from Barbra Sher in  the book, \"Wishcraft.\"  I thought about and described what my \"ideal day\" would be like.  Well . . . in my ideal day, I don't have to cook dinner, someone serves it to me and cleans up after it.  The reason is that I almost always get a second wind in the afternoon and I really resent having to stop mid project and cook dinner.   I also am getting to dislike meal planning because my husband eats what I cook for dinner, and when I ask him what he wants he almost never has any ideas, \"whatever\" is his stock reply, but then he rolls his eyes if I serve left overs or something vegetarian he doesn't like.  He doesn't realize that even though as a COURTESY to him I cook and eat meat, I don't like to, I prefer vegetarian food.  He thinks since vegetarianism isn't the norm, that meat eating isn't a burden or a compromise.  He has a singular perspective.  But then complains about tofu and lentils, both of which are a delicious and perfectly normal part of a vegetarian diet. Well I'm not going to get my personal vegetarian chef, but I thought maybe trying one of the meal delivery services might at least add a little fun to meal times.  I called a friend who has been doing it for years with Blue Apron, she encouraged me to try.  I chose \"Dinnerly\" because it was less expensive and I was not interested in meals being delivered pre-made wrapped in beaucoup plastic.  Dinnerly seemed the most local and least packaged. So far I have liked the meals a lot but am probably going to cancel.  Hubs thought the whole thing was silly and a waste of money.  I enjoyed not having to think much about dinner.  I was able to get some items I wouldn't buy in the store because I would have had to buy larger sizes and don't have the storage space.  I enjoyed the convenience of having everything pre-measured. Still, just too much plastic, although not dramatically more than the way things are mostly at a grocery store.  Try as I do, it is pretty hard to avoid plastic food containers.  About 75% of the produce was sealed in plastic.  Not all, but most.  In the store I have to use the plastic produce bags, even though I wash them and re-use some of them, so that wasn't a lot different.  Little individually packaged dry goods and sauces, as opposed to larger bulk containers, but still would be mostly plastic.  Hubs didn't much care for the vegetarian options but he is very negative.  But in the middle of the week he said he wanted chili, which was not on the menu, so we had to eat separate that night.  Weeks go by and he has no request, and then all of a sudden he wants chili with meat in it.  I get it, he just doesn't like to eat vegetarian, despite his saying otherwise.  Only once and a while, not on a regular basis.  I feel the opposite, meat is OK once and a while but not on a regular basis.  Yes of course I know how to make stuff that can just have additional meat added.  Just more cooking  for me and I don't enjoy cooking, just the eating part! Does anyone use a book that describes how to make your own vegetarian meal kits?  That was another thought I had, maybe making my own kit on Sundays.  I also thought about hiring someone to come in once a week and do meal prep for me.  Anyone ever tried that?  I think it would be hard to find someone who could do vegetarian around here.  I have a classmate who does that kind of thing, but she's a big meat eater, farm girl who does fantastic traditional foods but I would say probably not into lentils and tofu . . . I could come up with my own meal kits, but I really would love not to have to spend a lot of brain power/energy on thinking about this.  That's what I liked about Dinnerly, giving my cooking/meal planning brain a rest.  I have plenty of other things to occupy my brain right now.", "images": []}

title: Added Chlorine to new Diamond Brite Pool! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "michelle-barnes101", "author_name": "Michelle Barnes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/michelle-barnes101", "date": "2024-01-15", "text": "I recently had Diamond Brite applied to my pool, but wasn't clearly instructed on the aftercare process. I contacted my pool company but didn\u2019t set up an appointment in time and got stuck over a holiday weekend with no contact from my pool company on how to proceed. I don't know why I didn't go to the Diamond Brite site, but I panicked and went to my local pool store and explained the situation. They gave me 3 chemicals to put in the pool until the guy could come out. (Stabilizer, Muriatic Acid, and Chlorine). Now I read DO NOT add Chlorine. My pool company was not happy when they finally got back to me. How badly did I damage my pool? It's 3 days in and it looks great. (the water is a little cloudy from sanding on the patio and the reflection of the trees but I don't see any bad spots)", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7c52137b05a5b461_8439-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mystic-pools-llc-pfvwus-pf~881695109", "author_name": "Mystic Pools, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/swimming-pool-builders/mystic-pools-llc-pfvwus-pf~881695109", "date": "2024-01-16", "text": "3 important tests would be calcium hardness, pH and Total Alkalinity. Make adjustments as needed. I would not worry about a stabilizer. Chems should be dissolved in a bucket of pool water individually and added to the pool a little at a time. Muriatic acid is best to control pH and Total Alkalinity. It must be diluted and not poured in straight as it can harm the finish. I generally hold off as long as possible before adding chorine and, I will only use liquid chlorine initially. Most likely your area does not have a high demand for chlorine as we are in the winter months. So, I would say you're ok. What type/form of chlorine was added? Brush at least twice a day for 2 weeks. title: Tendances 2024 en décoration : Innovation et Durabilité à l'Honneur | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "florence-neron-pfvwfr-pf~1547321305", "author_name": "Florence Neron", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/interior-architects/florence-neron-pfvwfr-pf~1547321305", "date": "2024-01-16", "text": "En 2024, le monde de la d\u00e9coration int\u00e9rieure continue d'\u00e9voluer, int\u00e9grant des technologies innovantes et des principes de durabilit\u00e9. Explorons les tendances les plus en vogue qui transforment nos espaces de vie.  Le Retour du Naturel: Le design int\u00e9rieur de 2024 met \u00e0 l'honneur les mat\u00e9riaux naturels. Bois, pierre, et fibres organiques sont de plus en plus pris\u00e9s pour leur aspect chaleureux et leur durabilit\u00e9. La qualit\u00e9 est ainsi privil\u00e9gi\u00e9e. Bois : L'\u00c9l\u00e9gance Intemporelle Le bois, avec ses nuances riches et ses textures vari\u00e9es, reste un choix de pr\u00e9dilection pour apporter une touche d'\u00e9l\u00e9gance et de chaleur dans tout espace de vie. Qu'il s'agisse de meubles en ch\u00eane massif, de parquets en noyer ou de touches d\u00e9coratives en bambou, l'utilisation du bois dans la d\u00e9coration int\u00e9rieure est un hommage \u00e0 la beaut\u00e9 et \u00e0 la robustesse de la nature. Pierre : La Force Naturelle La pierre, depuis longtemps appr\u00e9ci\u00e9e pour sa solidit\u00e9 et son style unique, continue de gagner en popularit\u00e9. Les designers int\u00e9rieurs de 2024 int\u00e8grent des \u00e9l\u00e9ments en pierre naturelle tels que le granit, le marbre ou le calcaire pour cr\u00e9er des espaces \u00e0 la fois modernes et intemporels. Ces mat\u00e9riaux ne se d\u00e9modent pas et sont parfaits pour des surfaces telles que les plans de travail, les sols et les rev\u00eatements muraux. Fibres Organiques : La Touche \u00c9co-responsable Les fibres organiques comme le lin, le coton, ou le jute sont devenues des \u00e9l\u00e9ments incontournables dans la d\u00e9coration \u00e9cologique. Utilis\u00e9s pour les rev\u00eatements, les rideaux, les tapis et les accessoires, ces mat\u00e9riaux apportent une touche de douceur et de fra\u00eecheur, tout en respectant l'environnement. ---------------------------------- En r\u00e9sum\u00e9, la tendance du retour au naturel en 2024 souligne un d\u00e9sir croissant d'authenticit\u00e9, de durabilit\u00e9 et de connexion avec l'environnement naturel. Oh, joy, they said, we're now a zone 7 something. The maps are made of averages, and then someone chooses which years to average. That may work for annual crops. It's time to stop fooling ourselves. Talking to someone rose-oriented from France, he say he has three zones.  Tropical: where citrus fruir trees live and produce.  Where he lives: where citrus trees don't.  And a third zone where he wouldn't want to live. I remember reading about some 'zone' near Calgary Alberta Canada which was defined by what did survive there over time. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "fig-insanity", "author_name": "fig_insanity Z7b E TN", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fig-insanity", "date": "2024-01-16", "text": "One thing the zone map has NEVER taken into account is winter snow cover. Plants can grow in gardens covered with snow that won't survive in \"warmer\" zones, just because of the insulating properties of the snow they get. Tonight, my garden will experience the coldest temps we've seen since the early 2000's. BUT, unusually, there is an 8\" blanket over everything, so I'm not nearly as worried about my teas as I was Christmas of 2022 when we had a sudden drop from 50F to 4F in 36 hours, with NO snow and a brutal, continuous 30 mph wind. Also, as Diane B. so often reminds people that are technically in the same zone as her, her latitude makes a huge difference in her seasons, both in a shorter growing season, AND snow cover. I grow many of the same roses as Diane, usually with zero snow cover, and have to prune them drastically each Spring just to reach living wood. Surprisingly, against conventional wisdom, it's not *usually* the pure teas that suffer the most. So I do agree that we need a very localized map, tied to a plant data base of what WILL survive where. That would be ideal. A boy can dream. EDIT: As an aside, when I first started gardening, this area was considered a solid Z6. According to every reference that actually offered zone ratings, aucuba was NOT hardy here, but only to Z7. I've had one bloom so far, and it was quite yellow. But the first blooms on the florist roses usually aren't real true. It takes a few bloomings to get them to look like they're supposed to.  I buy most of my florist stems from Safeway. I love that they have the names and the sell by date. It makes it easy to see how fresh they are. I rarely buy ones that have sell by dates less than 2 days away. If they aren't fresh, the leaves will fall off and they won't root easily. Some tips for rooting them... make sure you tamp whatever soil medium you use very tightly, and when you get the stems put in the soil, make sure they are tamped down tightly again. Loose stems don't root. Leave at least 2 leaves on the stems, and I cut them at about 8\" length. The longer cuttings seem to root better and make a nice sized plant faster. And keep them well misted! You should get roots in 3-8 wks depending on the temperature. Mine are in a greenhouse and I had to get a heater to put in there in this extremely cold weather. main_question: {"author_id": "kitasei2", "author_name": "kitasei2", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kitasei2", "date": "2024-01-17", "text": "I have watched the Zimmerman video about pruning climbing roses nd am leftvwith a question.  If a (usually lower) lateral is left to climb vertically and becomes aa thick as a cane, it can tgen be treated aa a cane, correct? But can a thick lateral-turning-cane be cut back to a few inches like a lateral? I have climbers that I would like to keep fairly narrow and am training on French tree guards.   Thank you for your advice!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mad-gallica", "author_name": "mad_gallica (z5 Eastern NY)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mad-gallica", "date": "2024-01-17", "text": "What's the variety? Something I wish I had known when I started with climbers is that almost all hardy, repeat blooming climbers come out of two lineages - AgCanada kordesii, or New Dawn. Neither of these produce roses that can read, or are remotely cooperative when it comes to training. I would *love* to see a pruning tutorial tackle New Dawn, but it isn't going to happen because the presenter doesn't want to end up having to be rescued by the cameraman. So I have never seen anything about training climbing roses that doesn't come out of some sort of alternate reality. My best guess is that the rose Paul Zimmerman is trying to train in this video, is some sort of Noisette, which is going to have a very different growth habit from what I'm used to. To answer the question, of course you can cut them back, but there is a decent chance they will die off, or only produce very weak laterals.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "kitasei2", "author_name": "kitasei2", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kitasei2", "date": "2024-01-17", "text": "Gallica, I have Florentina, Quick Silver, Generous Gardener, Mme Carriere, Dublin Bay, and Iceberg.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "oldmoses", "author_name": "Moses, Pitt PA, cold W & hot-humid S, z6", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oldmoses", "date": "2024-01-18", "text": "You want to limit horizontal growth, right?  Train anything back as far as you want, then train new growth coming from the reduced canes in the direction you want as it extends and is the most flexible to cooperate.  Do the training right away as it is putting on size early on from spring on.  That way you have the growth growing in the direction that you want without having to force it as you would if you waited until it progressed to a hardening off stage later in the season.  At that time getting it to cooperate if you want to change its direction may be problematic. Moses", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "nippstress", "author_name": "nippstress - zone 5 Nebraska", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nippstress", "date": "2024-01-31", "text": "I have grown all the climbers you list and some of them are going to resist any attempts to keep them reined in. Even in what used to be my zone 5, my Mme. Alfred Carriere wanted to eat the south side of my house alive and bitterly resented any pruning by refusing to bloom on anything but old wood. Since she was marginally hardy in my zone, I only got blooms in one out of 5 year or so. In warmer zones she's happier and blooms longer, but also much huger. If you are training a climber vertically only without any horizontal growth, you run the risk of the plant blooming only on the ends of the canes. With my climbers, in order to get more lush bloom you need to train smaller canes growing vertically from horizontally trained canes. Yes, those laterals then become \"real\" canes when you train them sideways and more laterals grow from them. In that case, all the rose canes (\"real\" and lateral) all bloom at the end of the canes but since you have a lot of new canes from the horizontal it looks like you have a full round of blooms. If you're looking for a tall structure of a rose on your French Tree guards that has a small cluster of blooms at the top, then you can keep some of the other roses you mention more or less constrained on this structure. Dublin Bay and Quicksilver aren't huge climbers in my zone, and frankly both Iceberg climbing and Generous Gardener were weak growers and poor bloomers in my zone so they would barely climb here at all anyway. Florentina is very robust and a great bloomer when you train her horizontally, so I doubt it would last long on this structure, particularly straight upright. What you could do if you want more blooms is train the rose to gradually spiral around those tree guards. A happy Florentina will swamp those 42\" supports quickly however (any mood of MAC would swamp it even faster). I train my Florentina on 8 foot arches and it needs a pretty strong structure. Think mature canes with a diameter of a half dollar or so that get stiffer with time. Just my two cents - you can always give it a try and add a more firm support over time. Just don't plant them somewhere that you'll be disappointed or skewered if they grow more than is feasible on that support after a few years. Most climbers take a good 4 years to grow anywhere near their mature height so don't just them to be tame by their performance in their first couple of years. Cynthia", "images": []}}

title: How to match texture of painted patched area to rest of wall | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ruthann-05", "author_name": "Ruth -Ann", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ruthann-05", "date": "2024-01-18", "text": "As  part of reno work in my parent's house, some patches to existing walls were necessary. The areas were painted over to match the rest of the wall (which was last painted about 20-25 years ago). The texture of the patched area is different from  the rest of the wall; it is smooth while the rest of the wall just has  the roller \"texture.\" The contractor claims that the drywall is different than it was 50 yrs ago when the house was built and that rollers have also changed. What?? Maybe some rollers are different but not that much. And, given that this is reno of an older home you should use one that matches. This is drywall NOT plaster. I have patched and painted in this house before and have also had similar work done in my house which is from 1986. In all of these cases, the texture matches and the patched area doesn't stand out. Judging from other areas that were poorly patched and painted, I'm guessing that they may not have fanned out and may not have put enough pressure with the roller or enough paint on it or a combo. They also probably didn't cut larger than the affected area. But, I'm not a pro painter and wondered if anyone knows if and how I should tell them to fix it. Thanks.", "images": []}

title: preparing for squash this season | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kitasei2", "author_name": "kitasei2", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kitasei2", "date": "2024-01-18", "text": "Last season I sowed a variety of squashes in an area: kabocha, yellow crookneck, zucchini, and gourds. The result was a crop of huge bumpy squashes that were clearly crosses. I got nothing identifiable or edible. This confused me as I thought crosses would show up the following year, not the same season. I need a lesson in botany. And advice about how to plant squash in this area next year, if at all. Thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~278115867", "author_name": "beesneeds", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~278115867", "date": "2024-01-18", "text": "If you had only vines.... you didn't have yellow crooks or zukes. Those grow on bushes. You have stuff there that looks like overgrown ones, but that's not it if you had only vines. You don't appear to have kabocha in that lot either, it is a round smooth squash, and you don't have that. Kabocha also isn't a Japanese squash, what other Japanese squash were you growing? How did you grow these? Did you start them in pots with tags, put a mixed bunch in direct sown, what? It is sounding like you might have mixed up some things together. Perhaps some sprouted and others didn't, or some died off and others thrived. Something you can do this year is make sure you keep track of who you are getting seed from. Clearly tagging your seedlings and/or planting areas so you know for sure what you are growing where. Dont mix together seed- it can lead to a confusing muddle.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "theresa-peterson82", "author_name": "Theresa Peterson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/theresa-peterson82", "date": "2024-01-18", "text": "Let's look beyond the statement \"Corner pantries are bad\" and consider WHY this opinion is prevalent: - In general, corner pantries interrupt the work flow; that is, they throw a big honking obstacle in the middle of the room. - In general, the doors to corner pantries become obstacles themselves -- the door can literally block you from setting down the item on the counter /force you to walk around the door every time. - They aren't all that large, and a good bit of their space is wasted on that awkward corner. - The doors on corner pantries can be too small /uncomfortable. However, every rule has an exception, and I don't think your corner pantry's bad because - It's a reno, not a new build.  You have to work with what you have.  Sure, a larger, two-sided walk-in pantry would be better, but we don't always have every option.  This corner pantry is better than no pantry /better than sticking to cabinetry in that corner. - Your proposed corner pantry is at the end of your work space, so it isn't interrupting your counter top. - I would flip-flop the door /hinge the door the other direction so you can enter it /remove items \"towards\" the countertop and the main work area. - You can go with lazy susans in the corner to help with the awkward corner issue. - Finally, accept that this is a small pantry -- don't expect it to rival a huge walk-in.  Plan its contents carefully, and it'll work out fine. Other thoughts on this kitchen: - I'd eliminate the large massing with the duplicate ovens and tall cabinet.  That item is crowding the table and blocking light from the glass doors.  Visually, the door seems to be \"in a hole\".  Instead, I'd go with a practical range instead of the cooktop /add plain cabinetry near the door.  This would be an ideal place to store dishware -- right between the dishwasher and the table. - If you really need that tall pantry, I'd rather see it over by the refrigerator -- keep all that tall massing on the interior wall.  Could the door be scooted down a bit? - The island seems too small ... I'd like to see it grow by 50%. - The rectangular table doesn't seem to work in this space.  I'd rather see something oval /oriented the other direction.  Ovals are easier to walk around /no corners ... and that'll be nice near the door.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "3 of the plants Evve shows are Portulacaria, which have the same growth habit as Crassula. Is there any negative in issuing very shallow planters as opposed to taller ones with room for way more volume of soil? \"Negative\" is subjective in that the pot typically looks better, but shallow pots are more difficult to grow in because they typically have a much higher % of saturated soil after a thorough watering. This makes it essential to either choose plants very forgiving of being over-watered, or ensuring you're using a grow medium that holds so little excess water it makes it difficult to over-water. Most grow media based on fine ingredients (peat, coir, compost, composted forest products) are not good choices for shallow pots because they hold excessive amounts of water. Leveraging Advanced Technology Medical billing service providers use advanced technology to manage the billing process. title: The Importance of Interior Design in Workplace Productivity | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ahad-hashim-pfvwus-pf~1481285983", "author_name": "Ahad hashim", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/ahad-hashim-pfvwus-pf~1481285983", "date": "2024-01-20", "text": "Interior design plays a crucial role in enhancing workplace productivity. With the right design, employees feel more comfortable and motivated, resulting in increased efficiency and job satisfaction. That is why it's essential to hire professional interior designers who offer full service interior design and to create a perfect working environment. The Value of a Well-Planned Layout Strategic space planning is a cornerstone of effective interior design. The goal is to make the best possible use of available square footage to support various work modes. For instance, open-concept seating fosters collaboration, huddle rooms enable focused small-group work, and private offices allow for concentration without disruptions.Getting the layout right ensures smooth traffic flow while reducing noise and other distractions. This allows employees to navigate the office and locate colleagues easily. Adequate meeting and breakout areas are also key, so teams can gather without commandeering desks.Thoughtful touches like conveniently located supplies, muted acoustics, and access to natural light all contribute to an environment tailored for productivity. Full-service interior design firms account for these kinds of factors when envisioning and actualizing office designs. The Psychology of Color Choices Color palettes carry psychological implications that can dramatically influence workplace satisfaction on a subconscious level. Warm hues like red, orange, and yellow spark creativity, energy, optimism, and collaboration. Cool tones of blue, green, and violet evoke calmness, focus, and analytical thinking.Neutrals like black, white, and gray project an aura of sleek professionalism. Strategic use of color zoning helps strike the right balance for different functional spaces, branding goals, and corporate culture. Vibrant accent walls or furniture inject visual interest while reflective ceiling tiles and indirect lighting prevent sensory overload.Full-service interior designers understand how to wield color, lighting, and materials to sculpt aesthetically pleasing and emotionally uplifting workspaces. Employees are more engaged and satisfied when surrounded by environments that make them feel energized, relaxed, or inspired. Ergonomics and Overall Well Being Physical and mental well-being are intrinsically linked to productivity. Ergonomic furniture and equipment help reduce muscle fatigue, eye strain, repetitive motion injuries, and other problems associated with prolonged computer use. Height-adjustable desks allow switching between sitting and standing. Mirrored screens reduce glare while air purifiers maintain indoor air quality.Interior landscaping introduces natural elements like large leafy plants, moss walls, or water features. Exposure to living greenery has measurable benefits for concentration, stress reduction, and overall happiness. Such wellness-oriented design considerations demonstrate that companies care about employee health, comfort and quality of life while working. Fostering Community Through Design Communal areas for informal social gatherings also boost morale and engagement. Stylish cafeterias, lounge spaces, game rooms, and outdoor seating provide opportunities to strengthen interpersonal bonds. These humanizing touches remind team members that they are part of a cohesive organization and community. Tasteful Artwork and Branded Accents Interior design also represents a chance to reinforce brand identity through visual content. Showcasing products, imagery, and signage reflecting core values and aesthetics brings purpose and inspiration into the workspace. Local art displays and photography introduce originality while speaking to regional talent and community.Branded wall graphics, murals or dimensional lettering infuse company personality using texture, shape, typography, and color. Playful, creative flourishes humanize sterile corporate environments. When sensitively incorporated, bespoke design elements make employees proud to work in a one-of-a-kind office tailored to company culture. Hiring Specialized Professionals Given the scope of considerations involved, it is prudent to hire experienced full-service interior design consultants for office renovations or builds. They holistically analyze needs and preferences to translate concepts into spatially harmonious and branded environments. With expertise spanning architecture, ergonomics, acoustics, furnishing, color psychology, lighting, and project management, their input is invaluable.Some interior design firms even handle furnishings procurement and installation. The most talented designers meld aesthetic vision, technical skills, and client collaboration into signature, made-to-order spaces. Although their services are an investment, the benefits are multifold.   Conclusion To sum up, interior design plays a crucial role in enhancing workplace productivity. It is essential to designers to create an ideal working environment. Strategic space planning, appropriate color schemes, and furniture arrangement are some of the elements that can significantly impact employee efficiency.Moreover, interior design is not just limited to workplace productivity. It is equally important to consider interior design in home renovations and room makeovers. A well-designed home interior can increase productivity and create an inspiring environment. Therefore, it is recommended to seek the assistance of professional interior designers for home renovation projects and room makeovers.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/917298ce05ac12de_5838-w500-h286-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a4a280e205ac12de_5839-w500-h286-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

I used \"Dinnerly\" which I recommend, very good quality, instructions, packaging, choices, cost per serving, etc.  I can only speak to their vegetarian options.  The rest looked good though.  They offer variations on some of their meals which could be vegan or with animal products depending on what you choose.  I thought the fact that tofu was way more expensive than meat to be sad, but the same is reflected in store prices.  For a product made out of dead cheap soybeans, it sure is expensive.  Same with the fake meats, not a cost effective grocery item usually.  I eat them, but not every day.  Portions were ample, no complaints in that department. Meal one: Bok choy lo mein This was good, although lo mein isn't a favorite dish of mine.  I love bok choy, and having this meal encouraged me to buy it more often.  It's pricey but you don't use that much.  I didn't cook the lo mein noodles separately as instructed.  Instead, I stir fried the bok choy and scallions and then added chicken broth to the wok and cooked the noodles in the broth.  They thickened it as they cooked.  The recipe called for a poached egg in the dish but I used diced teriyaki marinated tofu.  It seemed skimpy on the vegetables so I added a package of frozen stir fry vegetables.  The plus for me on this meal was to encourage me to buy bok choy more often and use those precut and frozen  stir fry mixes for the ease.  I prefer buckwheat noodles also. Meal two: Roasted brussel sprouts and mushrooms in barbecue sauce served over scallion and garlic grits Again, a plus for me was the brussel sprouts, I don't make them often enough since they are expensive.  I had never made grits with garlic before, very good.  I usually just make plain polenta and serve a sauce over it, but I think adding scallions and garlic was great, along with cheese and butter at the end.  I added carrots to the roasted veggie mix.  An easy dish for me to repeat.  Also encouraged me to get back into roasting veggies, really warms up the kitchen! Meal three: Gluten free cheese ravioli with spinach Two items I don't often buy due to the large amount of plastic they come in, fresh pasta and baby spinach.  They don't sell gluten free fresh pastas at my local grocery, just dried ones, so this was a treat.  I learned an easy way of steaming spinach to add to the dish, just put it in the colander and drain the pasta over it, that wilts it enough to go into the dish, but still keeps a fresh taste.  Plus you can wash it ahead of time and drain in the same colander, so this meal didn't create a lot of dishes to wash. Meal four: Cuban picadillo with Impossible burger and jasmine rice. This is one of my favorite dishes, I usually use Morningstar farms fake meat crumbles, so this was one of my first tastes of the Impossible burger.  It was good, but the burgers came preformed and sealed separately in a large amount of plastic, so I would not have bought this on my own.  It also came with Cento tomato sauce, a brand I don't usually buy.  I buy the cheaper store brand.  I found the Cento to be of better taste/higher quality.  Not sure it made a huge difference, but some.  I loved not having to measure anything for this dish.  If I made it again on my own I'd make up a big batch of the stew and freeze it. Good quality olives too, something I don't usually get.  I only buy kalamata.  I had some left over corn and some sauteed sweet red pepper, which I added, those were good additions. Delish.  Even hubs said he liked it and he usually doesn't like anything with a sweet and sour vibe. Meal five: Roasted garbanzo beans in a Mediterranean themed chef salad Good but a little tart.  The dressing called for fresh squeezed lemon juice, which I almost never fuss with.  It was good but aggravated my GERD.  I had never roasted garbanzo beans before, what a revelation!  They were delish, even more nutty tasting than fresh cooked.  They kind of got lost in the salad though, which was heavy on the humus based dressing.  I had never used hummus to make dressing before, that was good.  I added a little goat cheese and green pepper.  The salad had fresh made croutons which you toasted in the oven along with the garbanzo beans.  Those were great!  Worth the extra trouble.  The salad featured a heart of romaine, one of my favorite salad greens.  I can get these in the store, but again, I never buy because they come pre-packaged in plastic.  Loved the dish but if I ever use romaine in a salad I buy the whole head and wash myself, not the pre packaged, pre-washed stuff. So overall, it was wasteful with all the packaging, but fun for me because it took a lot of the thinking out of the process and featured fancy foods I don't normally splurge on.  I also think given enough time I might be able to put together some of my own kits for some of these options, so it's a good way to collect a set of recipe ideas to tweak on your own later.", "images": []}

The smell seems most strong under the kitchen sink in the cupboard and under the dishwasher, which is right next to the sink. Sometimes we smell it outside the house right about the spot we smell it inside. The smell is close to the floor but wafts upward. Our boiler flue is nowhere near this area and we already checked for any clogging. We\u2019ve cleaned the dishwasher and disposal, pulled out the P trap to check for build-up, checked for evidence of leaks, checked for mold, nothing. A few more points: the underside of the dishwasher seems to smell particularly strong (not inside the unit but underneath if you pull it away from the wall). title: Community Engagement and Capacity Building for Sustainable Development | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "louis-day", "author_name": "Louis Day", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/louis-day", "date": "2024-01-21", "text": "Fostering Community Engagement and Capacity Building for Sustainable Development Introduction: Community engagement and capacity building are essential pillars of fostering sustainable development and creating resilient, thriving societies. These concepts emphasize the active participation of community members in decision-making processes and the development of their skills and resources. In this article, we will explore the significance of community engagement and capacity building, their interdependence, and the positive impact they can have on communities. Community Engagement: Community engagement is a dynamic process that involves the active participation of individuals, groups, and organizations within a community. It goes beyond traditional communication to ensure that community members are not just informed, but also empowered to contribute to shaping their own future. This involvement can take various forms, including public meetings, forums, surveys, and collaborative projects. Benefits of Community Engagement: Community Capacity Building: Community capacity building focuses on enhancing the skills, knowledge, and resources within a community to address its needs and challenges effectively. This process equips individuals and organizations with the tools they need to identify, plan, and implement sustainable solutions. Key Components of Community Capacity Building: Interdependence of Community Engagement and Capacity Building: Community engagement and capacity building are interdependent processes. Engaged communities are more likely to participate actively in capacity-building initiatives, and a well-equipped community is better positioned to engage meaningfully in decision-making processes. Colette is one climber that has a lot of side growth which I like and don't remove but have pruned a bit to keep in bounds.
