Virginia \u2022 zone 7A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dave-in_nova", "date": "2024-01-22", "text": "So go about 10\" x 10\"", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "Something I wrote years ago about what determines appropriate pot size, and why: Choosing an Appropriate Size Container How large a container \u2018can\u2019 or \u2018should\u2019 be, depends on the relationship between the mass of the plant material you are working with and your choice of grow media. We often concern ourselves with \"over-potting\" (using a container that is too large), but \"over-potting\" is a term that arises from a lack of a basic understanding about the relationship we will look at, which logically determines appropriate container size. It's often repeated that you should only move up one container size when \"potting-up\". The reasoning is, that when potting up to a container more than one size larger, the medium will remain wet too long and potentially cause root rot issues, or at a minimum, limited root function. In reality, it is the size/mass of the plant material you are working with, and the physical properties of the medium you choose that determines both the upper & lower limits of appropriate container size - not a formulaic upward progression of container sizes. In many cases, after root pruning a plant, it may even be appropriate to step down a container size or two, but as you will see, that also depends on the physical properties of the medium you choose. It's not uncommon for me, after a repot/root-pruning to pot in containers as small as 1/5 the size as that which the plant had been growing in prior to the work. Plants grown in \u2018slow\u2019 (slow-draining/water-retentive) media need to be grown in containers with smaller volumes so the plant can use water quickly, allowing air to return to the medium before root issues more serious than impaired root function/metabolism become a limiting factor. We know that the anaerobic (airless) conditions that accompany soggy media quickly kill fine roots and impair root function/metabolism. We also know smaller medium volumes and the root constriction that accompany them cause plants to both extend branches and gain o/a mass much more slowly - a bane if rapid growth is the goal - a boon if growth restriction and a compact plant are what you have your sights set on. Conversely, rampant growth can be had by growing in very large containers and in very fast (draining) media where frequent watering and fertilizing is required - so it's not that plants rebel at being potted into very large containers per se, but rather, they rebel at being potted into very large containers in a medium too slow and water-retentive. This is a key point. We know there is an inverse relationship between media particle size and the height of the perched water table (PWT) in containers. A PWT is water that fills spaces between soil particles and defies gravity by refusing to leave the pot. As particle size increases, the height of the PWT decreases, until at about a particle size of just under 1/8 inch, media will no longer hold perched water. If there is no perched water, the medium is ALWAYS well aerated, even when it is at container capacity (fully saturated). So, if you aim for a medium (like the gritty mix) composed primarily of particles larger than 1/16\", there is no upper limit to container size, other than what you can practically manage. The lower size limit will be determined by the medium volume's ability to allow room for roots to \u2019run\u2019 and to furnish water enough to sustain the plant between irrigations. Bearing heavily on this ability is the ratio of fine roots to coarse roots. It takes a minimum amount of fine rootage to support the canopy under high water demand. If the container is full of large roots, there may not be room for a sufficient volume of the fine roots that do all the water/nutrient delivery work, and the coarse roots, too. You can grow a very large plant in a very small container if the roots have been well managed and the lion's share of the rootage is fine. You can also grow very small plants, even seedlings, in seemingly inordinately large containers if the medium is fast (free-draining and well-aerated) enough that it holds no, or very little perched water. I have just offered clear illustration why the oft repeated advice to \u2018resist potting up more than one pot size at a time\u2019, only applies when using heavy, water-retentive media. Well-aerated media are not bound by the same restrictions. As the ht and volume of the perched water table are reduced, the potential for negative effects associated with over-potting are diminished in a direct relationship with the reduction - up to the point at which the soil holds no (or an insignificant amount) of perched water and over-potting pretty much becomes a non-issue. Al", "images": []}}

title: Dual flush or water-efficient toilets: Recommendations, experiences | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "barb-chamberlain97", "author_name": "Barb Chamberlain", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/barb-chamberlain97", "date": "2024-01-21", "text": "The discussions on dual-flush toilets are mostly older ones. I'm teeing up a new thread since plumbing technology continues to advance. We want a water-efficient toilet for conservation reasons. Older threads refer to the California testing site created because they had an incentive for switching out toilets but the site is dead (so don't follow this link https://www.map-testing.com/ but if you know where that information got archived please share that link). I've been reading up on dual-flush toilets here, on Consumer Reports, and in another review site. Some of the issues people identify aren't ones that show up in the specifications. For example, how much water refills in the bowl after flushing determines what hits porcelain, what hits water. Some models require multiple flushings or apparently can't really handle a larger load. And the list goes on. Features: -Comfort-height - Water-efficient; dual-flush would be great if it works well. - Base: I think our preference is for a wrapped or hidden base; need to confirm with our plumber that this would work. - Seat: Still debating round vs elongated seat; if the toilet had the other features we want that wouldn't be a deal-breaker. Soft-close seat would be ideal. - Material: Not plastic. The special finishes some offer would be nice. - Gravity feed: Quieter than the jet-assist models from what I've read and we don't have plumbing issues requiring a booster rocket for the launch; had the sewer line scoped when we bought 3 years ago. We *don't* need the high-end toilets with a comma in the price tag. The toilet we're replacing is a side effect/opportunity from a much larger remodel and we're nearing the end of the budget, but we would rather spend a couple of hundred dollars more than regret it and be replacing it in a few years. We're seeking value for dollars spent, not toilets that lift their lids by themselves and light the floor.", "images": []}

title: Rooted violet leaves : what now? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "linnea56chgo5b", "author_name": "linnea56 (zone 5b Chicago)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/linnea56chgo5b", "date": "2024-01-21", "text": "I was attempting to save my first ever violet by several means. This was back in November. I cut it off and repotted the trunk, and bagged the whole plant. It\u2019s still bagged, I have no idea how long this takes. I then stuck 4 leaves with short stems into rooting powder, then straight into violet potting mix with extra perlite added. Bagged the whole pot. .2 leaves have died and been removed. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "popmama", "author_name": "popmama (Colorado, USDA z5)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/popmama", "date": "2024-01-22", "text": "You can transition them to soil. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "erasmus-gw", "author_name": "erasmus_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/erasmus-gw", "date": "2024-01-22", "text": "I live in zone 7a also,  in NC.   Winters are usually not severe here though some years it can get down to as low as 4 degrees.   I grow between 350 and 400 roses and don't do any winter protecting.   I  am wary of piling anything up on stems whether grafted or not.  Vernon Rickard,  the late owner of Almost Heaven Roses,  who also lived in NC,   used to make wire cages around some of his roses and would fill those with fallen leaves.  But I never do that. When I first got into roses  I thought own-root plants were much easier to grow ,  had prettier shapes as plants,  and  thrived better for me than  prior grafted plants I had bought.   But  it could have been due to me  being introduced to some rose varieties that I had never tried before.   Perhaps they were just  more vigorous plants.  Also  I may have bought poor quality grafted plants like \" body bag\"  plants from Walmart.  It's hit or miss with those.   I've had some good luck with them but  bad luck as well. The hmf site  has tabs at the top of each rose page where you can click on  additional pictures ,  comments from people in different locales,  and  ratings for hardiness,  vigor,  disease resistance, etc. We've had a severe cold snap here but I am not devoting any time at all to worrying about my roses in the ground. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "3 of the plants Evve shows are Portulacaria, which have the same growth habit as Crassula. Is there any negative in issuing very shallow planters as opposed to taller ones with room for way more volume of soil? \"Negative\" is subjective in that the pot typically looks better, but shallow pots are more difficult to grow in because they typically have a much higher % of saturated soil after a thorough watering. This makes it essential to either choose plants very forgiving of being over-watered, or ensuring you're using a grow medium that holds so little excess water it makes it difficult to over-water. As you learn more about bonsai, you'll find practiced growers are very particular about their choice of grow medium, and alter the structure and components to suit individual plants.Most grow media based on fine ingredients (peat, coir, compost, composted forest products) are not good choices for shallow pots because they hold excessive amounts of water. For example, if you use a medium that supports 3\" of excess (perched) water at the pot's bottom, using that soil in a 3\" deep pot would find you growing in a soil that is 100% saturated after a thorough watering. It would be challenging for even skilled growers to maintain a jade or mini-jade (portulacaria) healthy in a situation like that. Notice how pot depth affects the amount of well-aerated soil a pot can hold after a thorough watering:   The pots are completely filled with soil. The shaded area represents excess (perched) water. Note - if you shift your focus to using the upright form of portulacaria for your bonsai endeavors (or other trees with naturally small leaves), you'll be able to produce a much better likeness of a tree you might find in nature. This is due to portulacaria's leaf size which is more proportionate to the scale of a smaller plant. main_question: {"author_id": "seniorballoon", "author_name": "SeniorBalloon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seniorballoon", "date": "2024-01-22", "text": "Pacific Northwest - Zone 7B I have been very bad about keeping track of the names of my clematis, and I'm now trying to get my brain around pruning practices. For instance, I have a President, (I know the name of this one, yay. :o) ) every year I have cut this back hard in late winter, early spring. It always flowers very nicely in mid to late summer.  I am reading today it is in Group B, which according to this web site - https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/clematis/group-two-pruning-guide and they advice pruning in late winter, early spring, but with the specific tip to do this- \"Remove dead or weak stems before growth begins. Check individual stems  from the top down until you reach a pair of healthy buds, and prune just  above them, removing the spindly or damaged growth above.\" I'm sure the Brits now what they're talking about, and I've also read that some Group B can be treated like Group C. Perhaps the President can handle either, but this year I'm thinking of following the RHS advice. I have another No ID clematis, that is in some bit of shade. it has never flowered much, but I've neglected it over the years. The last few years I've been pruning it back hard in late winter early spring and it hasn't flowered at all. It grows vigorously, and climbs 8 to 10 feet, but no flowers. While it could be the partly shady condition, I'm thinking it's in Group B, and one that doesn't like hard pruning at all, and I'll be trying the above RHS tip on that one.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2024-01-22", "text": "The division into individual pruning groups are just guidelines. At a previous garden I had way too many clems - around 60 or so - and there was no way I could keep track of who needed pruning when and how much. Other than the type 1's or no pruning required group - I treated them all the same - a late winter hard prune as if they were all type 3's. Other than delaying slightly the bloom period for the type 2's, when and how hard I pruned made NO impact on the flowering ability of the type 2's. IME, which includes decades of growing clematis in all its forms as well as working for a local major wholesale clematis grower, hard pruning of any clematis type will not affect bloomage....other than with respect to timing. Type 1's or old wood bloomers should be pruned back (if needed or desired) as soon after the initial bloom cycle as possible in order to allow sufficient regrowth and ripening of the wood for the next season's blooms. If hard pruning of a type 2 failed to produce any flowers, look to the timing issues or lack of sufficient sunlight. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "caroline-freedman75", "author_name": "Caroline Freedman", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/caroline-freedman75", "date": "2024-01-24", "text": "I'm no expert but it looks good to me! I am also currently re-doing a 1920s home and choose a slightly mushroomy color for the cabinets to move away from the stark white look. My cabinet designer included one glass front cabinet as well. The biggest would be the lower income.   Senior citizens typically have a set revenue, indicating that they might possess a smaller amount of funds to utilise compared to their working years. Downsizing and decluttering can aid in diminishing your costs and prolonging the lifespan of your finances. As you grow older, you might encounter health or mobility problems that render it more difficult to uphold a spacious residence or handle numerous belongings. If the response is affirmative, then it is worth retaining. If not, contemplate offering it to someone who may find value in it or transferring it to a beloved person who may derive more enjoyment from it. Make legacy gifts: Such gifts are significant belongings that carry emotional worth but can also be handed down to cherished individuals as ancestral treasures (perfect when decluttering items you may not want to throw away). Consider the costs: It is simple to downsize in terms of space, but downsizing in cost may be more complex. Create an inventory of all the expenditures you will encounter and establish a financial plan. This will assist you in determining if downsizing is financially viable. In conclusion, downsizing and decluttering can be a daunting task, but it is well worth the effort for retirees looking to simplify their lives and create more space for hobbies and activities like golfing. title: Insulating Behind Medicine Cabinet on Exterior Wall | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-528228756", "author_name": "HU-528228756", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-528228756", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "Looking for a good insulation method / material for the following situation: Recently completed new home. One of the medicine cabinets is on an exterior wall so it's it's got virtually no insulation inside the cabinet from exterior heat and cold. The cabinet is about 3-1/4 deep - so I'm guessing currently there is about a 1/2-inch at most of gap between the back of the medicine cabinet and the exterior sheeting (3-1/2 stud + thickness of drywall; plywood sheeting (Zip) then stone/stucco on exterior). I'm leaning towards pulling the cabinet out of the wall (dang finishing nails set deep into side studs!). Then cutting a 1\" to 1.5\" thick foam board to size and inserting in opening. Another option might be to get a couple cans of foam spray and filling the void then trimming it back to whatever thickness I can. Then frame an extra border around the opening to match the medicine cabinet wood with matching/stained 3/4 hardwood. The medicine cabinet would stand proud an additional 3/4\" from the wall.  But that would give me the extra space behind it to allow for some insulation: about 1\" to 1.5\". (I suppose, once removed, I could also cut down and rebuild the back panel of the medicine cab to make it a little more shallow - more work though) A 1-inch foam board shows R-4 or R-5 values depending on brand. Not as good as an insulated wall. But comparable to stud. And better than nothing - which is what I have now. Great Stuff canned foam shows R6 (per inch) - a little better - but trickier to work with and trim down to whatever thickness... Or maybe fiberglass batting could be compressed in there instead... Compression would reduce R value but might still be as good as or better than foam board...? QUESTION: Any better insulation materials to consider for this application? Or any preferred or to avoid from the ones I identified above? Thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-528228756", "author_name": "HU-528228756", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-528228756", "date": "2024-07-13", "text": "To follow up now that we have had a few triple digit days... Bottom Line: The solution to ad an inch of foam board behind the medicine cabinets worked great. --- After pulling the medicine cabinets - we (builder's rep and myself) installed 2 layers of 1/2\" foam boards (didn't find the 1\" locally). I also caulked around the edges of the foam boards thinking that might eliminate hot air drifting in. The builder's original cabinet maker perfectly matched the trim and stain with a second layer to fir the cabinet out 3/4\" or so. Everything fit back like a glove. Cosmetically it looks great. Yes the trim appears to be twice as thick but really it's not noticeable. It's partially covered by towel rings, I know it's there and I don't even notice it. So the average observer may never notice either. I found my IR thermometer and took some readings once we hit some 100s. With the indoor TStat at 78F the highest reading I was able to on the inside of the panel in early afternoon just after the exterior wall looses direct sun was 83F to 84F. That was the worst case scenario. After midday when the wall is in shade even with outside temps well above 100F, the surface temp on the back panel drops - eventually down to ambient 78 or 79F. The second cabinet had an exterior wall T in behind - so one half of the cabinet was exposed to exterior (no sun) and the other half to interior wall. It read 78 on the interior wall and 79F on the exterior wall. Interestingly, I had leave the cabinets shut all day and take these reading w/ my IR TStat immediately after opening at mid-day. Otherwise within just a few minutes of opening, the surface temps on the back panels quickly adjust to ambient air temps. For comparison other surface mounted cabinets mounted to various exterior walls in other parts of the house: They usually showed about 79F on their back panels, occasionally 80F. Simply touching the back panel of the medicine cabinet I cannot detect or 'feel' any warmth or heat coming thru whatsoever. Perhaps most important - none of the creams or heavier lotion items became in the least bit 'liquidy'. So bottom line is the solution to ad an inch of foam board behind the medicine cabinets worked great.", "images": []}}

title: Who here propagates mollis azaleas? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tete-a_tete", "author_name": "tete_a_tete", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tete-a_tete", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "And do you have a great method? I find them to be tricky but I know there is a secret to it, if I only knew it.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "The ARS offers this: \" Deciduous azaleas are very tricky to propagate from cuttings.  Take cuttings of deciduous azaleas when the new growth is soft and pliant.  This is often coincident with time of bloom in early June. The ability to root decreases rapidly as new growth matures.  Trim cuttings below a node (overall length of cuttings 3 to 5 inches) and dip in a rooting hormone containing fungicide.  Insert in a medium of 60% milled sphagnum peat moss and 40% horticultural perlite.  Usually bottom warmth of 75\u00b0F is used to encourage root growth.  In late August, transplant cuttings that are rooted and grown on in the greenhouse with supplementary light (14-hours a day) to prevent dormancy and induce new growth.  In the following fall, transfer to a cool, frost-free (35\u00b0F to 41\u00b0F) environment to induce dormancy.  As new growth develops in the spring, transfer plants to a shaded environment. Layering: This is the easiest form of propagation for the home gardener.  A lower branch is held down on soil (not mulch) with a stone.  A slit is cut in an area in contact with the soil and the cut is treated with a rooting hormone.  Then the cut area will sprout roots.  When the roots are developed enough to support the end of the branch, usually in 2 years, the rooted-branch is cut from the parent plant and transplanted.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "tete-a_tete", "author_name": "tete_a_tete", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tete-a_tete", "date": "2024-01-28", "text": "Thank you so much gardengal.", "images": []}}

title: hard freeze and beets | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2024-01-26", "text": "I always thought that beets were somewhat freeze tolerant. We had a bizarre couple of days when the temp went down to 15F. I mean, it hardly ever even freezes down here. I had beet seedlings that were an inch or so high. Even covered, they were destroyed. Interestingly, beets that were planted a week or two before but had not yet come up were also destroyed. They never came up. Interestingly, I am reading that seedlings are indeed less frost tolerant than mature plants. The \"antifreeze\" of salts, sugars, and other organic compounds haven't yet fully developed in seedlings. As an aside, beets can tolerate about half of the internal water being frozen as ice. title: Water Worker failing - what are my options? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "biondanonima", "author_name": "biondanonima (Zone 7a Hudson Valley)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/biondanonima", "date": "2024-01-27", "text": "I own a 125-year old house that was fully renovated by the previous owners. When we bought the house in 2016, we inquired about the presence of a large (86 gal) Water Worker in the basement, and were told that it was there to help increase water pressure. Previous owners claimed that the pressure issue was the city's fault and largely a result of our house being situated up hill from the city water source. Anyway, back then our water pressure in sink taps, showers, etc., was decent, but would drop off after about 15 minutes in the shower or running the hose outside. Now, we're lucky to get 3-4 minutes of good pressure in the showers before it drops precipitously. The Water Worker was manufactured in 2013, so no surprise it is failing, but I'm not sure that it was ever that effective given that we only got 15 mins of good water when it was relatively new. The previous owners took a LOT of shortcuts when renovating so I would imagine they went with the Water Worker as the cheapest, easiest solution to the problem. Is there anything else we can do? Would replacing the main solve the problem more permanently? How much might something like that cost? Thanks in advance for any advice!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2024-01-31", "text": "Yeah, I'm sorry about not catching it during inspection. A decent inspector should have caught it. The tank is a big \"Heads-up\" and the galvanized service line gives it away completely. A water utility has the responsibility to deliver water at suitable pressure - so the \"top of the hill\" excuse doesn't fly. The responsibility for the service line varies by utility. You should check with the utility. For some, the meter pit is outside and they are responsible for anything before the meter. For our utility, they are responsible for anything in the right-of-way (which is often several feet into a yard). Horizontal boring can be a thing - especially where there's a hill. They would have to come in under the electrical panel to avoid a 90 degree turn - or they would dig just that part of it to make the turn. Know that they will almost certainly come back with PEX or poly pipe (probably PEX) - meaning that it will not be usable as an electrical ground. You will need to install a ground rod (not difficult, but you need to do it) and bond your electrical stuff to it - including your copper plumbing. Electrical code calls for two grounding electrodes - although old houses often had just one. If you are installing a ground rod anyway, now's the time to make sure there are two grounding electrodes - and your water service will no longer be one of them. Again - if anyone so much as mentions lead pipe - check with the utility regarding federal funds for lead service line replacement. There was $15 billion to fund replacing all of it.", "images": []}}

Hi Ann, thanks for your question and yes you can. Because no \"transfer\" happens (where the tile pattern shows through the new floor) with laminate floors, it can be ideal to go over tiles. Things to consider though is 1) the tiles need to be level and no more than +/-3mm up and down over 3 metres, plus free from any bumps or lumps (as in physical textured highlights that stand \"up\" too much in the tiles) then 2) the added thickness. Generally decent laminate will start at 8mm and will usually go on a 2mm underlay, with the popular ranges now being 12mm that also sit on a 2mm underlay, meaning your new floor height will jump up between 10mm and 14mm. This could impact how the new floor intersects with existing carpet, existing doors, front and back entries and of course fridge cavities, dishwasher spaces etc. Do I need to screed over exiting an existing slabs before laying glued down vinyl planks? Hi blgreader, thanks for that and the answer is technically no, it is not required as a standard that must be done every time. However, vinyl planks, just like any floor, will perform better when the subfloor is level. In the case of LVT, there is also the consideration of needing to glue them down, which requires the floor to not just be level (see above for that definition), but also clean and dry and able to receive the adhesive. Because of this, it is common for vinyl installers to want to apply a skim coat which can assist in both cases, and in more severe cases, a levelling compound which will also renew the subfloor and allow the successful installation and longevity of the new LVT installation. Make sure your LVT is being hardset and not being glued with pressure sensitive adhesive. Moisture in your concrete slab is important to measure and manage, as it can break down the adhesive holding your LVT product in. Make sure you discuss moisture content of your subfloor with your chosen installer and mitigate that risk by assessing the MC. title: What is hybrid flooring? (get the facts not the hype) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "the-flooring-centre-au-pfvwau-pf~189431830", "author_name": "The Flooring Centre AU", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/flooring-contractors/the-flooring-centre-au-pfvwau-pf~189431830", "date": "2024-01-28", "text": "There is a lot of mis-information in Australia about Hybrid Flooring...here are the FACTS.   (Pictured above is the 9mm Lumina Longboard GEN 2 Hybrid that uses digital printing. Colour Twilight) Hybrid flooring launched in Australia in 2017 and was the result of efforts from a select group of professionals from three companies, being two importers and a retail group. Two of the main people involved in creating this category are the Co-Founders and Directors of our parent company so we are lucky to be able to provide this advice to you straight from the pioneers of this category in Australia rather than the pages and pages of mis-information and mis-truths that are plastered all over the internet and rolling from the tongues of slick salespeople Australia wide. Hybrid flooring is the category name used in Australia to describe an innovative range of flooring products that can trace it's history back to the 1st Generation of Hybrid flooring launched by Piet Dossche of USFloors in 2013. In 2013, it was discovered in a factory in Zhejiang province in China that a foamed Wood Plastic Composite (WPC) core could be extruded and then bonded to a Luxury Vinyl Plank (LVT) surface to create a new floating waterproof flooring system superior to regular vinyl planks (as it could be installed by almost anyone rather than relying on vinyl installers) and much better with moisture than traditional laminate floors. The term Hybrid was used in Australia to market the category as it most accurately portrays its new and inventive nature. It is a category, not a particular product. Hybrid is a floor category that describes floors that are not pure laminates, pure timbers or pure vinyls, but are combinations or iterations of developing technological advances. It is an ideal category name for new and emerging technologies as hybrid literally means \"of mixed character; composed of different elements\". In 2016 a new format of Hybrid flooring, what we refer to as 2nd Generation Hybrid was invented that refined the process by making it a one-step process to make the Hybrid flooring (rather than the 1st Generation where two separate products being a core and a surface were made then combined). The way this was done was to remove the wood flour content and the aeration of the core and rather extrude a Stone Plastic Composite (SPC) core made from limestone in the form of calcium carbonate and PVC and at the same time apply the decor and surface wear layer all on the one machine, making it more cost effective and faster to produce, meaning it was also less at the retail level for customers than the more labour intensive WPC 1st Generation option.   (Side profile of a 2nd Generation Hybrid Floor) The solid nature of the SPC meant it was originally marketed towards commercial settings in markets like North America whereas the WPC alternative was focused on the residential market. Australia largely skipped the 1st Generation Hybrid floors as the Australian market had experienced terrible outcomes with unstable click vinyl planks in previous years and so Australia only embraced Hybrid flooring in the back half of 2017 once the 2nd Generation products were developed and the brand new category created and launched. In or around 2018, a governing body emerged that the larger manufacturers signed up to and the naming conventions streamlined so that two main streams of Hybrid flooring were recognised, first being Expanded Polymer Core (EPC) which replaced WPC (as wood flour was no longer being used) and the \"expanded\" term accurately referred to the aeration of the core. The second was Solid Polymer Core (SPC) which clarified the often confusing terminology of Stone Plastic Composite, Stone Polymer Core and all the other iterations the market was seeing. \"Solid\" meaning it is not aerated and is solid. Both EPC and SPC are 2nd Generation Hybrid floors. There are various iterations of these and some brands claim to be \"next generation\" but look into it to see if they are or if it is a marketing spin. So, in general, 2nd Generation Hybrid floors are based around the concept of delivering a veneer of PVC protecting the picture of timber or stone bonded to a waterproof core that can be floated rather than stuck down. Are most of them good?....yes they are, but the category also has its limitations and is \"oversold\" as a miracle floor by those who don't know better (sometimes deliberately misleading, but more often just through ignorance) and pumped pretty hard on forums as it is relatively new and shiny. As the factories knew the products had it's limitations and naturally are always looking for ways to be more competitive, since 2017 factories have searched for ways to improve their Hybrid floors and experimented with various formats that included Mineral Fibre Board (MFB) and also attempted adding a veneer of real timber to an SPC core, known widely as VSPC. Another good example of these types of developments are the magnesium core boards referred to as an MGO product. Whilst factories in China were racing to develop new versions of Hybrid, KronoSwiss, one of the worlds largest producers of wood based building materials including laminate flooring, launched Corepel in the US market and was the first to properly launch what we refer to as a 3rd Generation (GEN 3) Hybrid floor. In our opinion, Corepel was the first commercially successful PVC FREE Hybrid floor made using majority wood based materials and still being waterproof, yet added extreme scratch resistance and at the same time fixed the issues around hot and cold (as it isn't made from plastic). It's core is referred to by KronoSwiss as a Durable Eco Composite (DEC) and it combines the waterproof factors of GEN 2 hybrid floors with the proven surface technology of higher end laminate floors that KronoSwiss are renowned for. Corepel is not currently available in Australia (at the time of writing this article). In 2023, a new 3rd Generation Durable Waterproof Core (DWC) was launched in Australia (and available at The Flooring Centre) to compliment the vast range of 2nd Generation Hybrid flooring options. This new GEN 3 DWC is a true 3rd generation PVC FREE Hybrid floor that ensures the wood fibres are wrapped in a wax encapsulation to protect them from moisture (yes, it is also waterproof) whilst allowing the use of highly scratch resistant laminate flooring technology to be used on the surface. GEN 3 Hybrid flooring is a significant leap forward for manufacturers and customers alike and is better for the environment as it uses no PVC in the core, surface or attached underlay (it's also VOC E-ZERO rated for total peace of mind). The HYPE around 2nd Generation Hybrid is a little out of control and the claims made by many retailers, both in stores and online, about the durability (the surface is only plastic and yes it DOES scratch) and suitability for many situations are inaccurate to say the least. In 2024, we are seeing global interest (at the big international trade shows such as Domotex in Hanover and Surfaces in Las Vegas) centre on PVC FREE flooring and most major manufacturers are starting to pour time and money into developing what we refer to as GEN 3 Hybrid floors that are more renewable, more durable and more attuned to the demands that families place on them. Examples of 2nd & 3rd Generation Hybrid Flooring Do you own research and make the right decision the first time & of course feel free to ask any questions here and we can assist you.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/817293ca05b5ddcc_7614-w500-h281-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3df2040d05b5e031_8227-w500-h333-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: (OT) Hey, it's almost February!  Garden report | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2024-01-29", "text": "The sun rose at 8 a.m. this morning.  I got up a little before 7 a.m., a noteworthy change after weeks of late rising; it may be due in part to finally being over the grim cold I caught shortly before Christmas, but the lengthening days certainly count as well.  We're entering the annual period, in fact, when my SAD-affected body perceives the increasing light and starts to lift toward spring. It's dry:  we've had no rain for weeks, and no snow this winter at all.  The low precipitation is now entering its fourth year, with no end in sight.  There's a high-pressure system sitting over our area, bringing air pollution and humidity but no rain;  DH and I went out yesterday and did a big watering of the plants we put in the ground in the fall, enough to keep them going for a while.  The weather system brings notably different effects at different elevations.  At our south-facing perch in the hills two days ago the morning was sunny and 50F, a mild springlike day; when DD and I got down to the train station in the plain, twenty miles or so away, the temperature had dropped twenty degrees, and we huddled deeper in our clothes in the freezing polluted fog.  This raw weather lasted the entire morning we were out; our return home brought us back up to the morning's beautiful mild weather.  However, in the last two days the smog has crept up here as well. Yesterday while watering I spotted some rootstock suckers I must dig out; that will be today's task I suppose, and further, endless cleanup.  I've been tidying along the northern boundary down in the big garden, just below the neighbors' hayfield.  There certainly is a contrast between its meager winter growth and the wild clumps of grass, roses, shrubs, and Italian cypresses on our side of the line:  soil still poor, but improving.  As I go further up the boundary I see that the ground is slumping, running from an old slide on our property and propagating up into the neighboring field.  This has been going on for many years, but I think the slump is currently active, which suggests the need for intervention.  More trees to plant: sturdy indomitable flowering ashes, nice-looking, quick to grow, long-lived, capable of growing in rock, as I've seen.  Actually, this unstable soil is part of the reason for my planting along the property line, along with aesthetics and environmentalism:  I don't want the neighbors' hillside to slide down and bury our garden.  It's a lot of hillside.  It does seem to be piling up here and there. We are firmly set in winter, but with the relatively mild temperatures and the sun, the warm climate roses have set new growth and buds.  'Cr\u00e9puscule' has been trying to flower through the winter, and 'Sanguinea' has a vivid bloom or two.  I'm enjoying the roses' fresh foliage, for all it's untimely.  Winter is our season of green grass, of course, and with the silvery olives and the dark Italian cypresses and some growing evergreen oaks and a few pines, there's quite a bit of green in the garden.  Few flowers, though the winter jasmine is coming into bloom, and the winter-flowering cherry, and, in shady places, the native and cultivated hellebores.  Oh, and Eleagnus x ebbingei, a fine shrub, its fragrance wafting in clove-scented waves; and the rosemary is coming into bloom.  Not so little happening, after all. The garden is a lot of smaller gardens within the big garden.  This fall we mainly worked on hedging.  We finished planting the hedges of what we call the Dutch Bed--now to see whether the plants survive this year--and the hedges backing up the Serbian Beds, or nearly; and we've almost finished planting the Small Triangle.  This last is important, as it's nearly complete (hurray!), and because it's an important part of the bulwark holding back the hill above it, or perhaps I'm flattering myself.  I don't know for sure.  The threat of land slumps and slides is very real, though. For tall hedges I use a lot of photinia and small-leaved privet, some winter honeysuckle and Symphoricarpos, an occasional plant of forsythia or Cotoneaster lacteus, native Viburnum lantana, lilac, hazelnut where I can get it to grow, Oregon grape for lower growth.  It's a matter of what I can easily and cheaply find in local nurseries--that will GROW FOR ME--or propagate for myself.  I want to continue hedge and tree planting next fall, though this may get derailed, as my plans so often do.  I want to plant more Eleagnus x ebbingei, but must order it from a nursery that sells liner plants, and lentisk, a plant not much known this far north, so will have to order it from a different nursery.  Our elevation, about 1400 ft, southwest orientation, and steep slope, mean that our garden is drier and warmer than much of the surrounding area.  This makes it possible, as well as desirable, to plant plants that are more widely grown in central and southern Italy than here.  Climate change also suggest that this is prudent.", "images": []}

title: Why is sewerage coming up through my bathroom drains during heavy rain | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ross-collin66", "author_name": "Ross Collin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ross-collin66", "date": "2024-01-29", "text": "I have recently suffered with raw sewerage coming up through my bathroom drains and also out of the shower drains during a large downpour, unfortunately it was quite substantial and ran right through the house. What would cause this and what can i do to prevent it happening again?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bigreader", "author_name": "bigreader", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bigreader", "date": "2024-01-29", "text": "You need a plumber which I\u2019m not. Storm water and sewage are too different systems.  If a rise in storm water is impacting your sewage then storm water is entering those pipes somehow. Generally this is an illegal stormwater discharge point by you or your neighbours into the sewage pipes. You may also have a broken sewer pipe allowing storm water to enter. My first call would be to the water authority that manages the sewer. Their advice will be free and they may check their pipes.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "bay-plumbing-and-drainage-pfvwau-pf~1799939346", "author_name": "Bay Plumbing & Drainage", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/plumbers/bay-plumbing-and-drainage-pfvwau-pf~1799939346", "date": "2024-02-09", "text": "Could be due to the ORG- overflow relief gully being installed to high and allowing the stormwater to drain into the sewer system and the 100mm house service not coping with the influx of water. Other things to look at are - blockages in the sewer system affecting discharge flow. - back flow from the mains sewer service pushing up into your property and discharging out the next lowest point- usually the shower if the ORG has been installed incorrectly or is capped To fix check overflow heights- The ORG should be installed so it sits at least 150 mm lower than the lowest fixture in the house. For example, your shower or toilet. It also needs to be least 75 mm above the ground to prevent stormwater flowing into your ORG. Also camera the sewer and stormy service. Consider installing a reflux valve in the sewer service. Camera cost to get checked usually $250, any decent local plumber will be able to locate fault fairly quickly.", "images": []}}

title: How does staffing agency scheduling software work? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-772295134", "author_name": "HU-772295134", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-772295134", "date": "2024-01-30", "text": "Staffing agency scheduling software streamlines the process of managing shifts and assigning personnel for temporary or contract positions. Here's a simplified overview of how it works: 1. Client and Job Requirements Input: The staffing agency scheduling software enters client requirements such as job specifications, shift timings, and necessary skills into the software. 2. Database Management: The software maintains a database of available workers, including their skills, qualifications, availability, and preferences. 3. Matching Algorithm: Using sophisticated algorithms, the software matches client requirements with available workers based on factors like skills, location, experience, and availability. 4. Scheduling and Assignment: Once a match is found, the software generates a schedule and assigns the appropriate worker to the job. 5. Communication: The software facilitates communication between the agency, clients, and workers, notifying them of shifts, changes, or updates via email, SMS, or app notifications. 6. Tracking and Reporting: It tracks worked hours, attendance, and performance metrics, providing comprehensive reports for clients and the agency. 7. Adaptability: Some advanced software can adapt to last-minute changes, finding replacements quickly if a scheduled worker cancels or doesn't show up. 8. Integration: It may integrate with other systems like payroll and accounting for seamless processing. Overall, staffing agency scheduling software automates and optimizes the process, ensuring efficient matching of available workers with client needs while minimizing scheduling conflicts and administrative overhead.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-353955525", "author_name": "Billsc", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-353955525", "date": "2024-02-05", "text": "Garden Mist, I'm going to jump in here again, with a few general pointers that may help.  Your plant looks healthy and growing well, so lets talk about some other things that will make it a more attractive house guest for you.  Hopefully you have taken James suggestion and not cut the bloom spike off yet.  let's talk about that a bit.  Bloom spikes when left alone after blooming usually turn brown and die back from the tip, farthest from the plant.  Unsightly!  Look at the flower spikes on your plant, The tip, out where the blooms were may already be turning brown, but close inspection will show that there is a scar on the stem where each bloom was attached.  The section where the blooms were will never do anything but die, so it can be cut off at any time.  Look at the bloom spike and notice, as you come down the spike toward the plant, the bloom scars will stop where the first flower was, and the bloom spike will begin to have joints.  At each joint there will be a little bump covered by a flap of plant tissue. That little bump is a growth node, and there are usually 1 to perhaps 4 of these.  If you cut the stem below (closest to the plant) the last bloom scar, and about an inch above the first growth node, you will may encourage one of the nodes on the spike to come to life, and produce a branch to the flower spike that will #1 bloom, or #2 produce a Keiki, or baby plant that is an exact genetic copy of mama, or #3 just go ahead and die.  Those choices are strictly up to the plant, it's genetic, you won't have much to say about the choice.  Remember, always cut with razor sharp tools that are clean and sterile.  Cut bloom spikes at an angle, do not crush--no scissors, or shears.  Now, your plant looks a bit nicer, no ragged dying tip on the bloom spike, and perhaps a new growth to brag about.  Have fun. Bill", "images": []}}
